New Release Spotlight

Reminders of Him: What the Film Can't Replicate

Colleen Hoover's 2022 novel became one of her most widely read — a romance built on grief and guilt, with a dual perspective that gives the reader simultaneous access to both Kenna's and Ledger's inner lives. Kenna Rowan walks out of prison after five years for the accident that killed her boyfriend Scotty, returns to the town where her four-year-old daughter Diem is being raised by Scotty's parents, and falls into a relationship with Ledger Ward — Scotty's best friend — that neither of them can justify to the people they love.

Vanessa Caswill's 2026 film, starring Maika Monroe and Tyriq Withers, premiered March 13 to respectful reviews. Monroe — known for horror roles in It Follows and Longlegs — brings a quality of watchful containment to Kenna that is interesting casting against type. The film is faithful in plot and structure. What it can't replicate is the novel's interiority: the letters Kenna writes to Scotty, the dual perspective that makes the romance feel earned, and Hoover's prose voice that carries the emotional weight of the CoHo formula.

This is a spotlight on what the adaptation gets right, what it loses, and why the reading order matters more here than in most cases.

Our Verdict
Read First: Book Wins
Hoover's dual perspective and Kenna's letters carry weight the film can't replicate.
Hoover wrote one of her most emotionally complete novels — grief and romance in careful balance, with a dual perspective that makes the reader feel both sides of the longing. Caswill made a faithful, well-cast film that loses some of the novel's interiority and retains its emotional core. The book is the richer experience. The film is worth seeing for Monroe's contained performance and Coon's dimensional Grace. Read first, then watch to see how the story translates — and where it doesn't.

The Novel: Why It Works

Hoover's CoHo formula — romance built on specific damage, with characters whose guilt and grief mirror each other — works consistently on the page because her prose voice carries the emotional weight. Reminders of Him is one of her most structurally sophisticated novels, alternating between Kenna's and Ledger's perspectives in a way that builds dramatic irony throughout. We know what each character is thinking and feeling even when they can't say it to each other, and that knowledge makes every scene more tense and more tender than it would be from a single perspective.

The letters Kenna writes to Scotty are the novel's most emotionally direct material. She writes to him throughout the story, processing her guilt, her love for Diem, her desperate hope to earn back the right to be a mother. These letters are where Hoover's voice is most present — raw, specific, and without the structural scaffolding of the romance plot. They're also where the novel earns its emotional climax. By the time Kenna gets what she's been working toward, the reader has lived inside her grief long enough to feel it as a genuine release.

The novel was criticized by some readers for romanticizing a relationship built on secrecy and disloyalty to Grace and Patrick. It's a fair critique. But Hoover doesn't pretend the relationship is without cost — the novel is about people making imperfect choices under the weight of grief, and it doesn't offer clean absolution. That moral complexity is part of what made it one of her most discussed books on BookTok.

The Film: What Caswill Gets Right

Caswill's adaptation is a sincere piece of work. The screenplay retains all major story beats and the central romance with fidelity. Monroe's reinterpretation of Kenna is the film's most interesting creative decision — where Hoover's Kenna is openly emotionally volatile, Monroe plays her grief as something held tightly, a woman who learned in prison not to show too much. It's a valid interpretation that changes the character's energy. Hoover's Kenna is raw; Monroe's is guarded. Both are damaged, but the texture is different.

Carrie Coon as Grace is the film's strongest performance. In the novel, Grace is an obstacle — Scotty's grieving mother who refuses to forgive Kenna or allow access to Diem, understandable in motivation but not fully developed. Coon brings depth that makes Grace more than an obstacle. Her anger is specific and lived-in; she's a mother protecting what's left of her son. Coon's performance adds weight to the film's final act in a way the novel doesn't quite match, and it's one of the genuine improvements the adaptation makes.

Tyriq Withers captures Ledger's quiet decency and the weight of divided loyalties with understated precision. The chemistry between Monroe and Withers works. The film handles Diem with the same care as the novel — Isla Merrick-Lawless is natural and unaffected in a role that could easily have been cloying.

What Gets Lost: The Dual Perspective and the Letters

The dual perspective is the first casualty. Caswill's screenplay condenses Hoover's alternating viewpoints into a more conventional single throughline, staying closer to Kenna's point of view. We lose Ledger's interior conflict — his specific guilt about being drawn to the woman responsible for his best friend's death, his loyalty to Grace and Patrick pulling against his growing feelings. The film compensates with Withers' performance, but performance can only do so much. Direct access to his thoughts is what made the novel's romance feel earned rather than convenient.

The letters are reduced to occasional voiceover, excerpting lines rather than presenting them whole. It's a practical choice — too much voiceover would feel literary and inert on screen — but it's a significant loss. The letters are where Hoover's prose voice is most present, and that voice is what carries the emotional weight of the story. Without it, the film's romance feels more like a well-executed genre exercise than an emotional experience. The CoHo formula requires the interiority to land. On screen, without it, the mechanics are visible in a way they aren't on the page.

Should You Read First or Watch First?

Read first. This is one of the clearer cases on the site. The novel's dual perspective and Kenna's letters are what give the story its emotional precision, and you can only lose your virginity to them once. If you watch the film first, you'll have the plot but not the interiority — and when you read the novel, the letters will feel like additions rather than the emotional core they actually are.

Read first and the film becomes a moving companion piece. You'll bring the novel's interior life to the screen, and you'll appreciate what Caswill and her cast accomplish within the constraints of the medium. Monroe's contained Kenna will be interesting precisely because you know how volatile Hoover's Kenna is — you'll understand what the performance is choosing to do differently. Coon's Grace will land harder because you'll know how much the novel leaves underdeveloped.

Watch first and you'll get a competent romance that may not fully explain why the book connected with so many readers. The film is good. The book is why the story matters. That's the order.

The CoHo Formula and Why This One Works

Hoover has been adapted twice in quick succession — It Ends With Us in 2024 and Reminders of Him in 2026 — and the results illustrate something consistent about her work. The CoHo formula is built on interiority. The romance works because of access to the characters' inner lives, not despite it. When you remove that access, what remains is competent genre fiction. The emotional specificity that makes her books connect with millions of readers doesn't survive the translation fully intact.

Reminders of Him is a better adaptation than It Ends With Us — it's more careful with the source material and better cast. But it faces the same fundamental problem. Hoover's voice is the product. You can't put it on screen. What you can do is make a sincere, faithful film that points back to the book — and that's what Caswill has done. Consider the film a very good trailer for the novel.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Reminders of Him based on a true story?

No. Colleen Hoover has stated that the novel is entirely fictional, though she drew on universal themes of grief, guilt, and second chances. The specifics of Kenna's incarceration and Scotty's death are invented, but the emotional landscape is grounded in real human experience.

How faithful is the 2026 film to the book?

Very faithful in plot and structure. Caswill's screenplay retains all major story beats, character arcs, and the central romance. The primary losses are the novel's dual perspective and the full text of Kenna's letters to Scotty, which provided much of the book's emotional interiority.

Why was Maika Monroe cast as Kenna?

Monroe, known primarily for horror roles in It Follows and Longlegs, brings a quality of watchful containment that reinterprets Kenna's grief as something held tightly rather than expressed openly. It's casting against type — her Kenna is quieter and more guarded than Hoover's, but no less damaged.

Does the film change the ending?

No. The film preserves the novel's ending, including Kenna's reunion with Diem and her tentative future with Ledger. The emotional beats are the same, though the film's visual language is necessarily less interior than Hoover's prose.

Should I read the book before watching the movie?

Yes. The novel's dual perspective and Kenna's letters are what give the story its emotional precision. The film is a sincere adaptation, but it loses some of that interiority. Reading first makes the film a moving companion piece rather than a replacement.

How does this compare to the It Ends With Us adaptation?

Reminders of Him is the stronger adaptation — more careful with the source material, better cast, and less compromised in its choices. It Ends With Us suffered from well-documented production conflicts; Reminders of Him doesn't. Both face the same fundamental challenge: Hoover's interiority doesn't translate to screen. Reminders handles that limitation more gracefully.
